title: What was the KGB?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the KGB, the Soviet Union's Committee for State Security. They trace its lineage from the Cheka (founded December 1917) through the OGPU and KGB to the FSB and SVR, and describe its dual role in foreign espionage and domestic surveillance, repression, and the Gulag. They cover its disinformation operations (Operation Pandora, fake organizations like the Monarchist Union of Central Russia), notable American spies (Aldrich Ames, Robert Hansen, John Anthony Walker Jr.), illegals and legends, its role in the 1991 coup against Gorbachev and the USSR's fall, Vladimir Putin's KGB and FSB background, and the poisonings of Litvinenko and Skripal in London. The episode closes with a book plug, reading suggestions, and a listener mail about heroin lozenges in a Canadian museum collection.

segments.title: Introduction to the KGB
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the KGB as a secret police and intelligence agency that kept the Communist Party in power through espionage, disinformation, and domestic repression. They explain the name, its headquarters at Lubyanka Square, and its successor agencies.

segments.title: KGB disinformation and 2016 election meddling
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Russian meddling in American politics, Operation Pandora in the 1960s, and fake personas posed as American groups. They cite Calder Walton's article on KGB disinformation and compare it with American covert operations.

segments.title: Cheka origins and the Monarchist Union infiltration
segments.summary: The Cheka was formed in December 1917 under Lenin as a secret police. The hosts trace its successor agencies and describe how it infiltrated and destroyed the Monarchist Union of Central Russia.

segments.title: Disinformation, World War II cooperation, and misinformation vs disinformation
segments.summary: The hosts describe wartime cooperation between the US, UK, and USSR and how it taught Soviets disinformation tactics. They define misinformation versus disinformation and discuss Soviet spying on the Manhattan Project.

segments.title: Illegals and legends
segments.summary: The hosts explain Soviet illegals who assumed false identities, sometimes based on dead infants' records, and the paranoia that rumors of sleeper agents can create.

segments.title: KGB size, structure, and directorates
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the KGB's staff size estimates and its main directorates covering foreign spies, political crimes, border protection, and state secrets. They describe monitoring of the military and foreigners.

segments.title: Domestic repression and the Gulag
segments.summary: The KGB's main focus was domestic surveillance and control of dissent, including phone tapping, arrests, and exile. The hosts discuss Solzhenitsyn's exile, the Gulag system, and estimates of deaths caused by the KGB.

segments.title: Sycophantic intelligence and KGB espionage success
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how fear under Stalin produced sycophantic intelligence that told leaders what they wanted to hear, and how the KGB's espionage helped the Soviets with weapons technology.

segments.title: American spies for the Soviets
segments.summary: The hosts describe American spies who sold secrets to the Soviets: Aldrich Ames, who exposed CIA sources; Robert Hansen, who sold classified documents; John Anthony Walker Jr., a Navy spy motivated by greed; and the Rosenbergs and Alger Hiss.

segments.title: Fall of the USSR, Putin, poisonings, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1991 KGB-led coup against Gorbachev and the Soviet breakup, Putin's KGB and FSB background, and the Litvinenko and Skripal poisonings. They close with reading recommendations and a listener mail about heroin lozenges in a Canadian museum.
